Hiya Harry,

Thanks for your response. I'm brand shiny new here so some of the terminology is a little lost on me and I know my reading of Price Action is a particular weak point. I know that FTR is Failure To Return, and I assume that that means 'to the Supply immediately above' / 'Demand immediately below', and that therefore it also indicates new actors front-running the prior Supply / Demand? So A7 is a good example of this and a high probability location for a short (had it not been retested already)? I can sort of see that pattern repeated on the left side of the chart around the pink line, but hasn't it then been consumed where you say "let's reload"?

I notice you ignore A9, which was that little blip (colossal blip when compared to your M1 flag!) just above (what I thought was new) Demand (labelled "consumed" on your chart), and which I thought looked like FTR (an inverted equivalent of A7, but with a loooong pause after the initial Demand). I'm guessing my first mistake was in where I placed my Base line, but I must have misread something else in doing so.

I put my bottom level for the Base higher up than the M1 flag, as I saw price was mostly reacting here, and thought it must be the last Demand before price turned back down. I figured that the two dips below my line to, and then through, the blue zone of your M1 flag must be successively lower pockets of new Demand (the second of which was my 'FTR'). Without saying it in so many words, that's why I placed the bottom of A8 where I did, figuring it was a flip. And also why I figured A9 might be good as it took that ('FTR') out. How should I have read this?

So, in the end, A7 would have been the best candidate if it wasn't already used. A8 is ok, if a little untidy, and also the potential victim of a bounce from broken A7. A9 is a non-starter because I've misread the Price Action here. And A6/A10, where you wrote "let's reload" is highly prospective (but wouldn't it likewise suffer from a bounce from A8? And where could I place my Stop?).

Apologies for having more questions (it seems I always have more questions:) ). I hope my description is clear when reviewing your chart below, I can re-edit a chart otherwise.

Hiya tradingjedi,

Don't be thanking me just yet - everything I observed might just be irrelevant tosh. just find I learn better through iteration:

1. Do it until I fail 2. Understand the nature of the failure and my part in it 3. Make appropriate changes to my method 4. Repeat

I've never been afraid of my mistakes, they've taught me far more than success ever has. So while I don't exactly invite them in for tea, I won't turn them away at the door. You can still profit from a mistake (if you're willing to admit to what you did wrong), it's just a reward of a different kind than cash.

Recently, I decided that it was time to reboot everything I thought I knew about trading, what I'd observed really wasn't working for me, so I blanked everything. I started by drawing random lines, seeing what happened around them, then deleting them and starting again. Each time I went through the loop I placed them with a bit more thought and care, which I could only do by learning from the good and bad of previous efforts.

I've got to a point where I think I get this subconsciously - some days I can read S / D and PA like a book, most days that book is written in a foreign language. But I need to drag the subconscious knowledge into my conscious so I can take a giant step up. The best way I know to do that is to 'formalise' what I've learned, by keeping on doing what works for me but in a public forum where everyone can point out the obvious stuff that I really can't see for myself, allowing me to ask ever better questions of myself.

The great benefit of a forum such as this is that everyone can accelerate their education, not only by doing their own work and having it assessed (an absolute necessity as you can only learn things your way), but by looking at the work of others and seeing how that is assessed. Win-win as they say!

Regards.

Spongy.

Hello all,

I don't think I'm entirely clear on the definition of FTR - I know it's Failure to Return, but I thought it meant item 1, whereas Cosmo's chart now makes me think it's item 2:

1. The Price Action being pointed to failed to return to the Demand below it or Supply above it before price shot out (ie it retraced a bit of the way back to its source but turned away before it could hit it) 2. Price shot out from the Price Action being pointed to and has since failed to return to it

If it's 1. then to me it's an interesting point of reference as it implies that buyers or sellers front ran the source of the move as price came back to it.

If it's 2. then what qualifier(s) are used to select a specific FTR over its brethren? In Cosmo's example below there's a clear level (pink line) and a strong move away from the FTR. But what if it weren't at a clear level?

Also, just in case it's dropped off anyone's radar, could someone take a look at my original post (24th April, 18:56hrs) and comment on the method and observations I made so I can learn from what I did right or wrong?

Thanks in advance for any comments.

Spongy.
